summary: Describes extensions for Transport Layer Security, including generic mechanisms for adding data to the TLS client and server hellos plus specific extensions built on them. They are backward compatible with clients and servers that lack them. It obsoleted RFC 3546 and updated RFC 4346, and was replaced by RFC 5246 and RFC 6066.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives TLS a way to carry extra information in the first messages of a connection, so that a feature can be added later without changing TLS itself. It defines the mechanism and then six extensions built on it, including one that tells the server which hostname the client wants and one that lets a small client negotiate shorter records. A client and a server that do not know about an extension can still connect.

subtitle: How new features are added to a TLS handshake without breaking the clients and servers already deployed.

tldr.problem: TLS had no way to carry extra information in the handshake, so a client could not tell a server which hostname it was contacting, and neither side could negotiate a smaller record size or a lighter way to check certificate status.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a list of typed extensions to the client and server hello messages, defines six extensions built on that list, and requires that a server only echo back an extension type the client actually sent.
tldr.outcome: The extensions are backwards compatible, so a client and a server that do not share them can still talk. RFC 4366 was obsoleted by RFC 5246 and RFC 6066 and updated by RFC 5746.

today: RFC 4366 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 5246 and RFC 6066, and it was updated by RFC 5746. The extension mechanism it defines is still the way TLS carries extra information during a handshake.

sections.title: Why TLS Needed Extensions
sections.content:
TLS is used in more kinds of environment than its original design anticipated, and many of them, such as wireless networks, have constraints that wired networks do not: limited bandwidth, limited computing power, limited memory and short battery life.

The extensions in this document extend the functionality of the TLS message formats. Other matters, such as adding new cipher suites, are deferred. Specifically, the extensions let a client give the server the name of the server it is contacting, so that one network address can serve several virtual servers; let both sides negotiate the largest fragment they will send; let a client send the location of its certificate rather than the certificate itself; let a client list the certificate authority root keys it holds; let both sides agree to use shorter message authentication codes; and let the server send certificate status information during the handshake instead of a revocation list.

Backwards compatibility rests on two rules. Servers must accept the extended client hello even when they do not understand the extension inside it, and no server response is mandatory when a client asks for extended functionality. A client that needs a feature the server does not have may abort the handshake, and some constrained clients are forced to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS was built for wired networks, and many of the networks it now runs on are short of bandwidth, memory or battery. This RFC adds a way for a client and a server to agree on extras during the handshake, without rewriting TLS. The rule that keeps it safe is simple: a server that does not recognise an extension ignores it and carries on.

sections.title: The Extension Mechanism
sections.content:
A client MAY send the extended client hello in place of the client hello. The extended format adds one field, client_hello_extension_list, holding a list of extensions. A server that supports the mechanism MUST accept a client hello in either the original or the extended form, MUST check that the data in the message matches one of those two forms exactly, and MUST send a fatal decode_error alert if it does not.

The server MAY send the extended server hello, which adds server_hello_extension_list, and only in response to an extended client hello. That restriction is what stops an extended server hello from breaking an existing client.

Each extension is a pair of fields: an extension_type that names the extension, and extension_data holding whatever that extension needs. For every extension type, including those defined later, the type MUST NOT appear in the extended server hello unless the same type appeared in the corresponding client hello, and a client that receives a type it did not request MUST abort the handshake. Extensions of different types may appear in any order, but there MUST NOT be more than one extension of the same type.

The document also adds two handshake messages, CertificateURL and CertificateStatus, and notes that an extended client hello may be sent both when starting a new session and when asking to resume one. If a session is resumed, the server MUST ignore the extensions and send a server hello containing none of the extension types, so the terms agreed in the original handshake apply to the resumed session.
sections.plainLanguage: The client hello and the server hello each gain an optional list of extensions. Each entry names a type and carries data for that type. The server may only repeat back a type the client actually sent, and it may only use the extended server hello if the client used the extended client hello. That is what makes an old client safe in front of a new server.

sections.title: The Six Extensions
sections.content:
Server Name Indication lets the client send the fully qualified DNS hostname it is contacting, encoded as UTF-8 with no trailing dot. Literal IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are not permitted. A server MAY use the name to choose which certificate to return, and in that case it SHALL include an empty server_name extension in its server hello. A server that understands the extension but does not recognise the name SHOULD send an unrecognized_name alert.

Maximum Fragment Length lets both sides negotiate a smaller maximum plaintext fragment than the fixed 2^14 bytes TLS normally uses. The allowed values are 2^9, 2^10, 2^11 and 2^12. A server that receives any other value MUST abort with an illegal_parameter alert, and so must a client that receives a different length from the one it asked for. Once negotiated, both sides MUST fragment immediately, including handshake messages, and the value holds for the whole session, including resumptions. With a negotiated length of 2^9, the record layer output can be at most 793 bytes: 5 bytes of headers, 512 bytes of application data, 256 bytes of padding and 20 bytes of MAC.

Client Certificate URLs let a client send the location of its certificate instead of the certificate itself, which saves memory on a constrained client. The server retrieves the chain from the URLs, and MUST check any SHA-1 hash it was given against what it fetched. Servers that support the extension MUST support the http: scheme, and the returned objects use the MIME types application/pkix-cert and application/pkix-pkipath.

Trusted CA Indication lets a client list the certificate authority root keys it holds, so the server can pick a chain it can actually use. Each key is identified as pre-agreed, by the SHA-1 hash of the key, by the X.509 distinguished name of the authority, or by the SHA-1 hash of a certificate carrying the key.

Truncated HMAC lets both sides agree to use only the first 10 bytes of the HMAC output as the message authentication code, saving 10 bytes per record. It has no effect on the pseudo-random function used for key derivation.

Certificate Status Request lets the client ask for certificate status information, such as an OCSP response, to be sent in the handshake instead of a certificate revocation list. The server returns a CertificateStatus message immediately after its Certificate message, and MUST NOT send it unless the client asked for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Six extensions are defined. One tells the server which name the client wants, so one address can serve many sites. One lets both sides agree on shorter records, which helps a slow link or a small device. One lets a client point at its certificate instead of sending it. One lists the certificate authority keys the client holds. One shortens the code that checks each record. One asks the server for a fresh statement about whether its certificate is still valid.

sections.title: New Error Alerts
sections.content:
Five alerts are added for use with the extensions. To avoid breaking existing clients and servers, these alerts MUST NOT be sent unless the sending party has received an extended hello from the party it is talking to.

unsupported_extension is sent by a client that finds an extension in the extended server hello that it did not put in its client hello, and is always fatal. unrecognized_name is sent by a server that receives a server_name request for a name it does not recognise, and MAY be fatal. certificate_unobtainable is sent by a server that cannot retrieve a certificate chain from the URLs the client supplied, and MAY be fatal. bad_certificate_status_response is sent by a client that receives an invalid certificate status response, and is always fatal. bad_certificate_hash_value is sent by a server when a fetched certificate does not match the hash the client gave, and is always fatal.
sections.plainLanguage: Five new error messages go with the extensions, and each one says what went wrong. The server may have sent something the client never asked for, the name may not have been recognised, the certificate may not have been fetched, its status may have been invalid, or it may not have matched its hash. All five may only be used after both sides have exchanged an extended hello.

sections.title: Defining New Extensions
sections.content:
The list of extension types is kept by IANA, and new values SHALL be defined only through the IETF Consensus process, because new features can interact with existing ones in ways that reduce the security of the whole protocol.

The RFC lists the considerations a designer should take into account. Each extension follows the convention that a server which understands an extension a client requested replies with an extension of the same type. A refusal to support a feature should be reported as a field in the server's extension response, while a genuine error condition should use an error alert. Extensions should be designed so that an attacker cannot force the use or the non-use of a feature by manipulating handshake messages; including the extension fields in the Finished message hashes is often enough, but extreme care is needed when an extension changes the meaning of handshake messages, because until the handshake is authenticated an active attacker can insert, remove or replace extensions. Finally, the RFC says it is possible to use extensions to change major aspects of TLS, such as cipher suite negotiation, but that this is not recommended, and that a new version of TLS is the right place for such a change, because the handshake algorithms protect against version rollback attacks based on the version number.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can propose a new extension, but it has to go through the normal IETF process, because two extensions that seem harmless on their own can combine badly. The RFC also warns designers to make sure that nobody can talk a peer into using or refusing a feature by tampering with the handshake. It says that a change as big as replacing cipher suite negotiation belongs in a new version of TLS rather than in an extension.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The level of security a client gets depends on what the server actually supports, so a client that requires a feature cannot assume it will get one.

For server_name, the RFC says implementations MUST ensure that no buffer overflow occurs whatever the length fields contain, and it recommends that server certificates not be issued for internationalized hostnames unless procedures exist to handle the risk of names that look alike when displayed.

For max_fragment_length, no new security complications arise, because TLS already requires implementations to handle fragmented handshake messages. Buffer sizing has to take the cipher suite and compression method into account.

For client_certificate_url, the RFC raises two issues. The first is whether a client should include certificate hashes; without them an attacker could obtain a valid certificate on the client's key that differs from the one the client meant to send. The second is that the server becomes a client of another URL protocol, so the client can prompt the server to connect to a URL of its choosing, which can be used to attack other hosts, to flood them, or to confirm the existence of internal hosts. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS that a server administrator must specifically enable this extension rather than have it on by default, and that URI protocols be enabled one by one.

For trusted_ca_keys, which certificate authority root keys a client holds may be confidential, so the extension should be used with care. For truncated_hmac, no significant weaknesses are currently known for HMAC with MD5 or SHA-1 truncated to 80 bits. For status_request, a server with a compromised key could pretend not to support the extension, so a client that requires OCSP validation SHOULD either contact the OCSP server directly or abort the handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: The main warning is about the certificate URL extension. It makes the server fetch a file that the client names, so a client can steer the server towards a host it should not reach. The RFC therefore says a server administrator should have to switch that extension on deliberately. For the rest, the main points are to avoid buffer problems and to treat the list of trusted certificate authorities as information that may be private. A server with a stolen key can also simply decline to send certificate status.

viz.caption: THE EXTENSION TYPES DEFINED IN RFC 4366

items.label: server_name
items.desc: The hostname the client is contacting.

items.label: max_fragment_length
items.desc: The largest fragment the client wants to send.

items.label: client_certificate_url
items.desc: The client sends the location of its certificate.

items.label: trusted_ca_keys
items.desc: The certificate authority root keys the client holds.

items.label: truncated_hmac
items.desc: Both sides agree to use 80-bit message authentication codes.

items.label: status_request
items.desc: The client asks for certificate status information in the handshake.

viz.caption: HOW AN EXTENSION IS OFFERED AND ACCEPTED (RFC 4366 SECTION 2.3)

messages.label: CLIENT HELLO
messages.note: The client lists the extensions it wants. The list may be empty.

messages.label: SERVER HELLO
messages.note: The server repeats only the extension types the client sent.

items.label: unsupported_extension
items.desc: The server sent an extension the client never asked for. Always fatal.

items.label: certificate_unobtainable
items.desc: The server could not fetch the certificate chain from the URLs given.

items.label: unrecognized_name
items.desc: The server does not recognise the name in the server_name extension.

items.label: bad_certificate_status_response
items.desc: The client received an invalid certificate status response. Always fatal.

items.label: bad_certificate_hash_value
items.desc: A fetched certificate did not match the hash the client supplied. Always fatal.
